Verification against Nestimate

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/verification.Rmd
verification.Rmd

A network statistic is only as trustworthy as its implementation. The similarity measures used to normalize co-occurrence counts have short formulas (van Eck & Waltman, 2009), but an implementation has to make many small decisions around them: how a transaction that lists an item twice is counted, whether the diagonal of the matrix holds item frequencies or zeros, which items survive a frequency filter, and in which order a threshold and a normalization are applied. Two implementations that agree on the formulas can still disagree on the numbers.

Nestimate contains an independent implementation of the same eight similarity measures in its own cooccurrence() function, written for its network-estimation framework. This guide compares the two on the data bundled with cooccure and shows that, once two documented conventions are aligned, they return the same weight matrix for every measure. The same comparison is kept in the package repository (tests/equivalence/test-nestimate-equivalence.R) and runs in continuous integration, on hand-built inputs in all five input formats both packages read, with frequency and weight filters, and on 40 randomly generated networks, so that the two cannot drift apart unnoticed. It is not part of the tests shipped to CRAN, so that a change in one package cannot fail the other’s check.

library(cooccure)

Both packages export a function called cooccurrence(), and they return different classes. Nestimate is therefore not attached here; every call to it is written as Nestimate::cooccurrence().

packageVersion("Nestimate")
#> [1] '0.9.24'

The comparison below was rendered against this version of Nestimate.

Data

Two bundled tables, in two input formats, supply the networks:

  • movies, a delimited format: one row per film, with the column genres holding the film’s genres separated by commas. Genres are the items and films the transactions; 1,000 films, 22 genres.
  • actors, a long format: one row per actor and film, with actor as the item and the film identifier tconst as the transaction; 624 actors in 401 films.

Two helpers that return comparable matrices

The two packages store their networks differently: cooccure returns an edge list whose matrix is read with as_matrix(), and Nestimate returns a netobject that holds the matrix. The first helper returns the cooccure matrix; the second returns the Nestimate matrix with the diagonal set to zero, since cooccure never stores self co-occurrence.

cooccure_matrix <- function(...) {
  as_matrix(cooccure::cooccurrence(...))
}

nestimate_matrix <- function(..., diagonal = FALSE) {
  m <- as.matrix(Nestimate::cooccurrence(..., diagonal = diagonal)$weights)
  diag(m) <- 0
  m
}

A third helper aligns the two matrices on their item names and returns the largest absolute difference between any two cells, and a fourth applies it to every similarity measure, returning one row per measure.

max_difference <- function(a, b) {
  items <- sort(rownames(a))
  stopifnot("the two networks hold different items" =
              setequal(rownames(a), rownames(b)))
  max(abs(a[items, items] - b[items, items]))
}

compare_measures <- function(...) {
  measures <- c("none", "jaccard", "cosine", "inclusion", "association",
                "dice", "equivalence", "relative")
  rows <- lapply(measures, function(s) {
    a <- cooccure_matrix(..., similarity = s)
    b <- nestimate_matrix(..., similarity = s)
    data.frame(similarity = s, items = nrow(a),
               max_abs_difference = max_difference(a, b))
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

Do the two packages agree on every similarity measure?

The genre network of the movies table is built with each of the eight measures by both packages, and the matrices are compared cell by cell.

compare_measures(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",")
#>    similarity items max_abs_difference
#> 1        none    22           0.00e+00
#> 2     jaccard    22           0.00e+00
#> 3      cosine    22           5.55e-17
#> 4   inclusion    22           0.00e+00
#> 5 association    22           0.00e+00
#> 6        dice    22           0.00e+00
#> 7 equivalence    22           0.00e+00
#> 8    relative    22           0.00e+00

Both packages find the same 22 genres for every measure. Seven of the eight measures agree exactly; for cosine the largest difference is of the order of 10-17, which is floating-point rounding from computing a square root in a different order, far below any meaningful difference in a similarity between 0 and 1.

The actor network is larger, 624 items and more than 4,000 edges, and comes from a long table rather than a delimited column.

compare_measures(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst")
#>    similarity items max_abs_difference
#> 1        none   624           0.00e+00
#> 2     jaccard   624           0.00e+00
#> 3      cosine   624           2.22e-16
#> 4   inclusion   624           0.00e+00
#> 5 association   624           0.00e+00
#> 6        dice   624           0.00e+00
#> 7 equivalence   624           0.00e+00
#> 8    relative   624           0.00e+00

The result is the same: every measure agrees to within 10-15, and cosine is again the only one with a non-zero difference.

Do filters give the same network?

Frequency and weight filters are where implementations most often part ways, because a filter can be applied before or after normalization. Here only genres in at least 20 films are kept, and Jaccard weights below 0.1 are dropped.

max_difference(
  cooccure_matrix(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                  similarity = "jaccard", min_occur = 20, threshold = 0.1),
  nestimate_matrix(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                   similarity = "jaccard", min_occur = 20, threshold = 0.1)
)
#> [1] 0

The filtered networks are identical: both packages remove rare items before counting and apply the weight threshold after the similarity measure.

Where the conventions differ

Two documented conventions differ between the packages, and both must be aligned before the numbers can match.

The diagonal

By default Nestimate stores each item’s frequency on the diagonal of the matrix (diagonal = TRUE), while cooccure always sets it to zero. For seven measures this changes only the diagonal, which the helper above zeroes. For relative it changes every cell: relative divides each row by its sum, and with the diagonal kept, the item’s own frequency is part of that sum.

max_difference(
  cooccure_matrix(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                  similarity = "relative"),
  nestimate_matrix(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                   similarity = "relative", diagonal = TRUE)
)
#> [1] 0.5

With the diagonal kept, the off-diagonal relative weights differ by up to 0.5. With diagonal = FALSE, as in the comparisons above, they agree exactly. The two packages therefore implement the same measure; the difference is in which co-occurrences count toward an item’s total.

Ties at the top_n cut

top_n keeps the heaviest edges. When several edges tie at the cut, cooccure truncates to exactly top_n edges and Nestimate keeps every edge tied with the last one. In the genre network, three pairs have an inclusion weight of 1, so the two packages return a different number of edges for top_n = 1.

cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
             similarity = "inclusion", top_n = 3)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 3 edges | density: 0.0130 | mean degree: 0.2727 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: inclusion | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 231 | isolates: 17
#> # top nodes: News(deg=2,str=2), Documentary(deg=1,str=1), Drama(deg=1,str=1), History(deg=1,str=1), Western(deg=1,str=1)
#>         from      to weight count
#>  Documentary    News      1     1
#>      History    News      1     1
#>        Drama Western      1     1

These are the three tied pairs. With top_n = 1, cooccure keeps the first of them and Nestimate keeps all three; the edges cooccure keeps are always a subset of those Nestimate keeps, with the same weights.

Direction of relative

relative is the only asymmetric measure: the weight from genre A to genre B is the share of A’s co-occurrences that involve B, which is not the share of B’s co-occurrences that involve A. Both packages store the asymmetric matrix compared above. cooccure returns one edge per direction and marks the network as directed, and so does Nestimate from version 1.0.11 onward.

genre_shares <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                             similarity = "relative")
print(genre_shares, n = 4)
#> # cooccurrence: 22 nodes, 258 directed edges | density: 0.5584 | mean degree: 23.4545 | 1000 transactions
#> # similarity: relative | counting: full
#> # possible edges: 462 | isolates: 0
#> # top nodes: Drama(deg=40,str=7.551), Comedy(deg=38,str=3.216), Action(deg=34,str=2.686), Romance(deg=34,str=1.847), Adventure(deg=30,str=2.104)
#>     from          to weight count
#>  Western       Drama  1.000     1
#>  Romance       Drama  0.553   131
#>      War       Drama  0.509    27
#>     News Documentary  0.500     1
#> # ... 254 more edges

The header reports directed edges: the 129 genre pairs give 258 directed edges. The strongest runs from Western to Drama with a weight of 1, because the single Western film is also tagged Drama and nothing else. The two directions of one pair can differ widely, as the Drama and Romance pair shows.

subset(as.data.frame(genre_shares),
       from %in% c("Drama", "Romance") & to %in% c("Drama", "Romance"))
#>       from      to weight count
#> 2  Romance   Drama  0.553   131
#> 44   Drama Romance  0.161   131

More than half (0.553) of Romance’s co-occurrences are with Drama, but only 0.161 of Drama’s co-occurrences are with Romance, because Drama co-occurs with almost every other genre. The raw count, 131 films, is the same in both directions.

What the comparison covers

The comparison establishes that, given the same transactions, the two packages compute the same weights. It does not test input parsing that only one package offers, such as the sliding windows, attention counting, event logs and aggregate_by of cooccure; those are checked in tests/testthat/test-cooccurrence.R against values computed by hand. For the choice between the measures themselves, see the guide to similarity measures.

References

van Eck, N. J., & Waltman, L. (2009). How to normalize cooccurrence data? An analysis of some well-known similarity measures. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 60(8), 1635–1651. https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.21075
